# **The impact of evaluation and accountability on academic ** **careers**
Katia Caballero ^(a) , Tony Harland ^(b) , Navé Wald ^(b) and Javier Mula-Falcón ^(a)
a Faculty of Education Sciences, University of Granada, Granada, Spain; ^(b) Higher Education Development Centre, University of Otago, Otago, New Zealand
#### **ABSTRACT **
This article examines the work experiences of academics in Spanish universities with respect to how individuals are affected by the complex requirements of neoliberal compliance and a culture of endogamy, often referred to as 'academic inbreeding'. The need to evaluate and be accountable for most aspects of academic work is relatively new in Spain and presently poorly understood. Compliance systems are usually introduced to enhance the quality of work, hold academics accountable for what they do, and provide a merit-based system for careers. However, in Spain, there is doubt that these objectives are being achieved. In our study, nineteen academics were interviewed about these issues. The majority felt that the evaluation systems were not fit for purpose and because of endogamy, academic merit was not the sole measure of a successful academic career. These outcomes have significant implications for quality and standards in this higher education system and we will argue that both issues need to be dealt with in a broader conversation about quality and the purposes of a university education.
#### **ARTICLE HISTORY**
Received 25 September 2023 Accepted 11 March 2024
#### **KEYWORDS **
Academic career; accountability; inbreeding; evaluation; neoliberalism
#### **Introduction**
The background to this study is the continuing reform of Spanish higher education. In the post-Franco era, in 1978, the Spanish Constitution ensured that university autonomy was recognized in law (art. 27.10), and in 1983 the University Reform Act (*Ley de * *Reforma Universitaria*), sought improvements to ensure that universities could operate as fully independent institutions. The sector then underwent a series of major legislative changes, largely driven by national and local government initiatives, and these still reverberate today affecting the work required of academics. There have been continuous changes to accountability, hiring and regulating progression through academic careers. Overall, the career system is not easy to navigate for both potential and established academics, but currently very little is known about how this is experienced. The sector, like universities across the world, has been subject to the neoliberal turn as it moves to mass

This article has been published under the Journal's transparent peer-review policy. Anonymised peer review reports of the submitted manuscript can be accessed under supplemental material online at [https://doi.org/10.1080/21568235.](https://doi.org/10.1080/21568235.2024.2331116) [2024.2331116](https://doi.org/10.1080/21568235.2024.2331116).
higher education, with the logic that institutions are now market-driven businesses subject to an audit culture (Sutton [2017](#page-17-0)). As part of this system, academics need to provide evidence of competence to attain different goals and they have become 'measured' professionals (Peseta, Barrie, and McLean [2017)](#page-17-1). Evaluations of one type or another seem to be ubiquitous in academic careers, not just in Spain but worldwide, nearly to an obsessional level. How academics experience accountability and the impact of evaluation is currently poorly understood, and in this paper, we examine these issues through the professional life histories of academic staff. We present empirical data from academics who share their accounts of working in Spanish public universities and in doing so explore how historical structural changes have influenced both individual choice and job satisfaction, and so provide new insights into both the experiences and identities of university teachers and researchers. The question guiding the research was 'how do academics experience evaluations of practice and what are the impacts on their academic identity?'
#### **Working in Spanish higher education**
The current higher education system in Spain is unique and does not align well with any other countries within the European Union or the wider English-speaking world. Mora and Vidal [(2005](#page-17-2)) provide a detailed history of the reforms of Spanish Higher Education and show a pattern of constant change in what has become a fragmented public system. These authors make the case that reforms and decentralization have created a sector with conflict between universities, regional and central government. Prior to the 1983 University Reform Act, the universities were elite state agencies. After the Act, they became much more autonomous, to the extent that they could design their own programmes and have some say in their own affairs. At this time, regional governments took over responsibility for institutions and so formal control shifted markedly. Importantly, staff were no longer part of the national state, and according to Mora and Vidal they now 'belonged' to each university (136). However, tenured academics remained as civil servants and members of a national body, rather than their institution, while regional bodies financed their own universities. According to these authors, it is this complexity that creates the potential for conflict. One outcome has been that universities are now creating new lower-ranked positions without tenure and the academic status of a civil servant. Sanchez-Ferrer ([1997)](#page-17-3) critically examined these reforms and argued that autonomy and self-regulation did not lead to higher-quality university services. This author attributes this failure partly to problems with the Act, but he also uses the neoliberal argument that there was a lack of exposure to free market competition between universities, which would provide incentives to strive for greater quality. At the time of his writing, university funding and careers were assured regardless of performance and both localism (as preference for one's own institution) and endogamy (as the practice of creating discrete autonomous academic groups) were seen as antithetical to quality. Sanchez-Ferrer suggested that new evaluation procedures for accountability would not increase quality, nor counter endogamy.
The next major reform was the 2001 University Ordinance Law (*Ley Orgánica de Uni**versidades*), which, for the purposes of this paper, brought in the requirement that tenured academics obtain a national qualification before being appointed. Overseeing
this was a new National Agency for Quality Assessment and Accreditation (*Agencia * *Nacional de Evaluación de la Calidad y Acreditación*, ANECA) which also had responsibility (alongside regional government) for quality assurance and accreditation of various aspects of university operations (Vidal [2003](#page-17-4)). In part, this was prompted by the Bologna Process (Bologna Declaration [1999](#page-16-0)) and the formation of the European Higher Education Area (see Neave and Maassen [2007)](#page-17-5) that sought, amongst other goals, to have a comparable degree system across the European Union (Ríos[ 2015](#page-17-6)). This change required new systems of quality assurance that were also later revised with the 2007 *Ley Orgánica * *de Modificación de la Ley Orgánica de Universidades *and with the current *Ley Orgánica * *del Sistema Universitario *enacted in 2023.
ANECA also accredits academics with a process that requires an examination that assesses an individual's curriculum, teaching and research. Accreditation is necessary to become a tenured civil servant, be appointed at *Contratado Doctor *(Senior Lecturer/Associate Professor), *Profesor Titular *(Associate Professor) or be promoted to *Catedrático de Universidad *(Full Professor). For the new academic, they must obtain a university post and acquire experience and hours in teaching, and show research success, before applying for civil service status. Regional agencies under the umbrella of ANECA can also provide accreditation for lower levels of employment ([Table 1](#page-3-0)).
With respect to salaries and incentives for academic performance, 'Sexenios' (6-year evaluation periods) were introduced to measure research quality (see Marini [2018](#page-17-7)) but only permanent academics can apply to ANECA for these (through its National Commission for the Assessment of Research Activity, CNEAI) (Artés, Pedraja-Chaparro, and del Mar Salinas-Jiménez [2017](#page-16-1); Marini [2018)](#page-17-7). If high enough standards are reached, then a salary increase is given but success also provides status and advantages for career progression. In addition, there are the older more established 'Quinquenios' (5 years) which give a salary increase to a wider range of academics, based on the evaluation of length of teaching service. However, this is not always available to staff across the sector. Finally, 'Transferencia' is a newer independent evaluation for third mission activities (transfer of knowledge and service to industry and society, every 6 years) (Marini [2018](#page-17-7); Sánchez-Barrioluengo [2014](#page-17-8)). This activity has been added to the *Sexenio *for those who may not meet the requirements for traditional research outputs. Currently, the evaluation treats each major field differently and an academic in a particular field must learn exactly what is required for success.

An academic applies for the evaluation of their teaching, research and knowledge transfer voluntarily. If successful, then there is a salary increase and *Sexenios *open the door for participation in master's and doctorate supervision, and have PhD students and fellowships associated with the academic. It is also seen as positive for obtaining research grants and so opens many more possibilities for constructing a research career. Obtaining regional or national accreditation for tenure or civil service status does not require *Sexenios *or *Quinquenios *but it would not be logical for an academic to have the evidence for success in accreditation and not to have applied for a *Sexenio*. ANECA examination for *Contratado Doctor*, *Titular de Universidad *and *Catedrático * *de Universidad *appears to be hierarchical, but a level can be passed over and it is possible to get a higher accreditation. For example, *Ayudante Doctor *can be accredited for *Titular * *de Universidad *if they meet the required criteria. With respect to *Quinquenio*, the university funds success with a pay rise although at present not all universities have the same criteria; nevertheless, ANECA is seeking to standardize this through its *Docentia * programme.
#### **Theoretical framework**
In this work, we use accountability theory in the context of neoliberal reform (Metz [2011](#page-17-9)). In principle, academics are held to account by those in power for aspects of their work. They are expected to take responsibility for their decisions and actions, and be answerable to stakeholders. Accountability is part of neoliberal ideology: when the state cannot privatize a public institution, it evaluates its activities to ensure there is an equivalence to freemarket competitive pressures that are intended to drive individuals to success (Harland [2016)](#page-16-2). This method of control has replaced earlier models of trust and working for the public good with neoliberal's individualized performance targets and the measurement of academic work (Olssen [2021)](#page-17-10). Measurement, however, allows universities to employ merit-based systems on which to determine salary levels and make decisions about career progression (Kelchen [2018](#page-17-11)). Although academic work is complex, practice is typically translated into what can be measured, primarily with numerical data, and when this is required by the university and different agencies, it can distort practice because it is impossible to genuinely 'measure' many important aspects of what academics do and value in their work. As such, one consequence of measurement, even when this is partial, is that academics focus on what is required of the evaluations to achieve their goals, which may then not align with quality research and teaching, or a sense of what education is for. Biesta [(2010)](#page-16-3) argues that questions of quality, effectiveness and accountability have even changed the discourse of higher education and what is now missing is the debate on what constitutes a good education or the question of 'what is an education for?' (2). As such, accountability may have failed in much of its intent while still having a wide effect on academics and their work (Marini [2018)](#page-17-7). Although neoliberal forms of accountability are relatively new in Spain, many other countries will be undergoing similar developments that transform university culture.
Accountability needs to recognize political, social and cultural contextual factors (Gómez and Valdés [2019)](#page-16-4). In Spanish higher education, one of the most important issues impacting academic work is endogamy. Endogamy (*Endogamia*) is mainly, but not exclusively, 'academic inbreeding' or hiring one's own postgraduates (Altbach,
Yudkevich, and Rumbley[ 2015;](#page-15-0) Horta[ 2022;](#page-16-5) Mora[ 2015)](#page-17-12). It is seen as a form of corruption by Rodilla ([1995)](#page-17-13), who claims that internal candidates are often appointed to a position regardless of a more suitable candidate being available. This was seen as detrimental to scientific research and innovation (Horta [2013)](#page-16-6) as well as to the universities' credibility and social mission (Horta [2022)](#page-16-5). Mora ([2015](#page-17-12)), on the other hand, claims that it 'is not perceived as a serious problem among Spanish university staff and leaders' (207). In this view, it may have benefits in terms of knowing a candidate's previous education abilities, experiences and social fit within a group (Balyer and Bakay[ 2022](#page-16-7)). Yet, it is still problematic if it is antithetical to a merit-based career system and when it precludes hiring the most talented person for the job. However, endogamy has a wider socio-anthropological significance than its narrower biological meaning of inbreeding. Essentially, it denotes 'a form of group closure' where individuals demarcate factions along cultural similarities (Kalmijn [1998,](#page-16-8) 396) thus reinforcing loyalty to that group.
The relationship between accountability and academic inbreeding (and patronage) is key to this paper, and it is not sufficiently explored in the literature. Academic inbreeding is seen as a longstanding and global phenomenon (Horta [2022)](#page-16-5), which is indicative of its ability to persist even with the proliferation of accountability and audit measures that were meant to increase transparency around decision-making and performance indicators. If this is accepted, then in this context, endogamy can make other aspects of accountability and evaluation seems pointless because, using the same neoliberal logic, their bureaucratic burden is inefficient and not cost-effective. Therefore, Rodilla's ([1995)](#page-17-13) call for policies that support a fairer system of appointment and career progression in universities is still relevant today.
## **Methods**
For this study, we used a qualitative methodology that sought to gain detailed insights into the participants' experiences and thoughts. Participants were recruited from earlier research by Mula-Falcón and Caballero [(2023](#page-17-14)) on perceptions of academic work. In their study, a survey questionnaire was sent to all academics working in nine public universities and 2183 responded. The survey was delivered by e-mail and as a part of the message an invitation was included asking if participants would like to take part in further research and these volunteers have provided the data for the present study. There were 24 replies and we were able to include nineteen [(Table 2](#page-6-0)). To avoid bias in participant selection, this was a self-selecting process. Yet, a social sciences background is dominant among participants, nearly half had no permanent employment status, and most were early or mid-career academics in their 30s and 40s. These should be noted as possible limitations of the study.
We used semi-structured interviews that each lasted between two and three hours. The extended interviews allowed a careful exploration of the participants' experiences of becoming and practising as an academic. This research technique allowed both interviewers and interviewees to mutually develop their ideas, and encouraged interviewees to explore and unpack their subjective experiences (Daniel and Harland[ 2018](#page-16-9)). The interviews centred on experiences of evaluation of academic work. All were asked about the impact of evaluation on their teaching, research, knowledge transfer, obtaining an academic position and career progression, as well as their broader working context.

Informed consent was granted to us after each participant was advised about the research purpose, the study requirements, their right to confidentiality, and the possibility of withdrawing from the research at any time. Male/female pseudonyms are used to ensure anonymity and any potential identifying information has been omitted. For the analysis, we started with our theoretical lenses and then adopted an interpretive-paradigm and an inductive process (Thomas [2006)](#page-17-15). This paradigm reflects an ontological position that reality is subjective and an epistemological view that knowledge is unique to participants, and mediated to readers by the researchers (Daniel and Harland [2018](#page-16-9)). Each interview transcript was analysed independently by three of the authors and Nvivo was used. Agreement was reached on the major ideas that emerged in relation to the evaluation of teaching, research, and transference, which reflect the evaluation system in Spain. For reporting data, we sometimes refer to academic titles when they help illustrate an argument.
#### **Results and discussion**
It was clear from the data that a career in academia was highly individualistic and competitive, an observation reported in many studies that have examined the neoliberal impacts on university work (Heath and Burdon [2013;](#page-16-10) Morrissey [2015)](#page-17-16). However, there was a layer of complexity superimposed on all work, as most academics needed some form of patronage to gain access to an academic job and for a successful career, rather than through a wholly merit-based system. The participants' accounts showed that most were stressed by adverse working conditions that were mostly outside of an individual's control. Only two participants seemed fully satisfied with their careers to date, but for the rest, the lack of job satisfaction was not about teaching or research *per se *but the impact of evaluation on these activities. Evaluation created a difficult working environment, which included job security (or insecurity), access to resources, achievement recognition and rewards (Shin and Jung [2014](#page-17-17)). It was clear that the audit culture and current compliance requirements were a major part of this. Accountability,
[FIGURE: see LR.R41_fig05.jpg]
nearly exclusively through evaluation exercises, resulted in undesirable behavioural changes and dealing with these came at a personal cost to individuals. We report the outcomes of the analysis in two sections to illustrate these ideas:
- (1) Evaluation and the measured academic - (2) Access to the university, endogamy and power relations
#### *1. Evaluation and the measured academic*
Although technically voluntary, evaluations were seen as compulsory as they were required for achieving academic and career goals which included attaining a first position, gaining tenure, civil servant status and career progression to high rank (see [Table 1](#page-3-0)). The three main areas of work evaluated were oriented to two specific purposes:
- (1) Access and career promotion based on the accreditation of specific components of teaching, research and transference (depending on the desired academic rank); - (2) Obtaining salary increases and other economic incentives that, in the case of research, also give access to certain academic privileges (see [Table 3](#page-7-0)).
We examine the data in three sub-sections and discuss what participants had to say about the evaluation of teaching, research and transference (or 'third mission', which is relatively new for Spanish higher education).
#### *Teaching*
Accreditation required the evaluation of teaching in which a set of indicators were assessed. These included teaching hours, subjects taught, student evaluations, teaching publications, and participation in teaching innovation projects. Evaluation was seen as the right thing to do, and it was accepted that teachers should be accountable. However, participants were very clear that what was measured bore little relevance to what really happens in the classroom (González-Calvo et al. [2020](#page-16-11)) and Victoria thought the evaluation criteria were 'completely out of touch with reality'. ANECA's *Docentia *programme is aimed at standardizing the evaluation of teaching quality, but the impression was that an actual measure of quality did not matter, so long as

a teacher reached the minimum number of hours required with respect to academic rank. For Caroline: 'The quality of your teaching does not matter and at most the quality of your teaching is measured by student surveys that leave a lot to be desired'. For Linda: 'the skills that ANECA imposes on me do not make me a better or worse teacher; I don't take them into account, and I abide by other values in the classroom, really'. And so: 'Teaching is not improved by the current programme, that is, the accreditation system today does not have teaching as its objective' (Sophie).
Student satisfaction questionnaires were distributed by the universities to generate evaluation reports for accreditation or the application for five-year terms. These also received much criticism from participants because, on the one hand, they did not faithfully reflect the performance of the teachers and, on the other, did not have clear consequences (neither positive nor negative) for practice. Harvey [(2002,](#page-16-12) 245) has argued that evaluations tend to support the *status quo *and that 'evaluators appear to be preoccupied with the method of evaluation rather than the substance'. This author argues that evaluation also fails the student learning experience. This idea was expressed in different ways in our study:
I am a good teacher when I go to the classroom and manage to teach people; all the rest are flourishes (…) despite the fact that I do very well, I don't think it accounts for whether I teach well. And I think that the picaresque occurs; if you like them or you evaluate well, then you are a good teacher. (Barbara)
Teacher quality surveys, what are they for? (…) is that they are useless. It doesn't matter if you fail or pass it … . (Emma)
Also, several respondents mentioned that the *Quinquenios *were not achieving their goal of rewarding quality teaching. Monica, for example, argued that:
… we all get the same amount of five-year teaching bonuses, which are called *Quinquenios*, no matter how you teach. So that really burns you. Seeing you running around, answering students, taking good care of them, seeing that they evaluate you wonderfully and yet there are no other prizes.
Overall, evaluation did not improve quality and in practice, the whole evaluative system provided a disincentive to this. This phenomenon has been described as 'vanilla' teaching, when teaching just needs be good enough (Harland and Wald [2018](#page-16-13)). Monica works for reward (because there is one) but as this goes to everyone for teaching it has lost its power to drive behaviour. At the same time, she appears to be calling for evaluations that differentiate between teachers or for more types of reward. If we compare this with the practice of assessing student work, if the assessment cannot differentiate between the quality of this work, then the assessment fails. To deal with such failure, some participants suggested the evaluation tools should be more nuanced and more targeted. Doing so is likely to increase the magnitude of the task and so the bureaucratic burden, but not the quality of teaching. Nor will it address the main problem of evaluations where the focus is on measuring the teacher and teaching when the impact on student learning is ignored (Harvey [2002](#page-16-12)). Yet academics still believed that there were steps that could be taken to better assess teaching quality and for this to have a positive impact on staff. A qualitative approach to
evaluation was suggested and John thought that evaluation should be designed as an instrument solely for improvement and not as a threat or punishment. However, the teaching evaluation system must be viewed in relation to other academic activities and teaching itself was seen as a secondary academic activity that was completely relegated to research. Alexander thought that in his career 'Teaching counts very little' and Emma suggested that many 'don't care about teaching and no, they don't value it either, I don't feel like they value teaching'. Emma, as an early career academic, did value teaching but recognized that priority should be given to research:
… we are focused on research, on obtaining funds, on obtaining investments, money, but I think that teaching is being left a bit aside and I think that we are a university centre that we have to give priority to teaching, quality teaching.
#### *Research evaluation*
The evaluation of research was related to the number of articles published and their impact. Research was seen as the most important activity for most academics with respect to careers. There is currently a desire in Spain to improve the overall culture and quality of research (Ion and Castro Ceacero [2017](#page-16-14)) and ANECA is the main government agency for measuring and evaluating this. It provides a centrally managed system, and this was thought to guarantee a level of transparency and rigour. None of the participants questioned the logic of the accreditation provided by this organization; however, there were many sentiments against how ANECA went about its business, and Caroline described it as 'Big Brother'.
One of the most questioned aspects of research evaluation was the reliance on the quantity of publications and the quality of journals targeted. Emma noted that:
If we do not publish JCR [Journal Citation Reports, Web of Knowledge], the research is useless and there are many very interesting investigations or articles that use them more to base your teaching on that scientific evidence than many Q1 [Journal ranking in top 25%] and I think that we give a lot of weight to the JCR, to the JCR research, but there is quality research that is not published there.
Linda shared this sentiment, saying that 'Of course, it is better to publish in Q1 … for ANECA it is better research, but for me it is not, that is, I have work published in worse journals, according to ANECA criteria, which are good works'.
There was general agreement that the more publications, the more possibilities there were for access to academic positions and promotion. At the same time, it was recognized that this created a lot of competition in publishing and often a failure to meet personal expectations. Some participants referred to the difficulty of responding to the evaluation criteria while maintaining a balance with other professional activities and the impact it had on personal lives. For instance: 'Since I have already obtained accreditation, the criteria seem good to me, but it is true that they are difficult. It is difficult, and also difficult to manage, that is, to make it compatible with the family' (Susan).
It was suggested that pressure to publish had led to some unethical strategies to accelerate or obtain successful results for access or promotion. Jack wondered if some indulged in this behaviour:
how many people there are who have been promoted, even professors, publishing and paying in well-positioned journals that have turned out to be predatory. Is that quality?
[FIGURE: see LR.R41_fig06.jpg]
And now those articles are no longer valid, but those people have already been promoted and have put themselves ahead of all the others.
#### He then added,
One more thing: a clear strategy is to publish a few good articles and a lot of bad articles. Otherwise, it is impossible to compete in today's university. Because to get into the places there are two options: either you have a lot of CV, or a lot of friends.
First, it seems that if these strategies work, then the ANECA quality criteria are not rigorous enough, and second, if these behaviours are replicated across the sector, this type of research evaluation will gradually create a mediocre research culture, rather than help intensify research or reach internationally determined standards (Ion and Castro Ceacero [2017)](#page-16-14). A related issue was that research funding prioritization alongside the eagerness to publish in journals of high impact forced academics to modify their focus of interest or to alternate between what was valued and what was desired by the system. For Daniel:
Above all, it loses the researcher, who is the most important thing, who is at the centre of the research. They may lose the freedom they have to develop a topic slowly or to enjoy it, because that is the important part for one to get to the bottom of the topic, to enjoy it … well, if that takes up too much time, it can be seen as a line that is not suitable for promotion. You have to get results, even if that means giving up things you like better. That's the problem I see with the system …
The research evaluation system itself was also seen as unstable in that every few years the criteria were reviewed and modified. Changes generated a certain restlessness and insecurity among staff. Caroline said that: 'For starters, stop changing the criteria, please, stop changing the criteria; (…) the feeling is that when you reach the goal, the goal moves'. In relation to this, Daniel argued that:
The motivation for why the rules of the game change so much every three to four years should be examined in detail. What is the dark motive behind it? Why do the criteria for being a researcher change one way or another? Is it that science is not the same? Why do those levels change? (…) It is disconcerting that one plays some rules of the game and then they change them.
Regularly changing the criteria supports an argument put forward by Muñoz-García ([2019)](#page-17-18) who suggests that external requirements for research performance are primarily about neoliberal regulation. In this context, an individual's relationship to knowledge will shift towards those who determine it is changing worth, which can be seen as a form of 'intellectual endogamy' (24), a recognized phenomenon in the academic inbreeding literature (Horta [2022)](#page-16-5).
#### *Transfer*
At the time of the study Transfer was the aspect of evaluation in which participants showed the least interest. In 2018, the National Commission for the Evaluation of Research Activity (ANECA Resolution of November 14) introduced a pilot project on the evaluation of knowledge transfer and innovation by university teaching and research staff from public research organizations. The requirements of what can be considered as third mission activities are still being outlined, but Susan questioned the possibility of developing a quality practice in all three academic functions: ' … all
three at the same time, yes, but with quality, poof, there is always something that you leave aside. Always. Or that you don't do it as well as you'd like'. If systems of evaluation for transfer or third mission are to be further developed for all disciplines to sit alongside the evaluation of teaching and research, then great care will need to be taken. In their survey of Spanish universities, Gonzalez-Sanchez, Gutierrez-Lopez, and Barrachina Palanca [(2022](#page-16-15)) found that transfer activities came from intrinsic motivation and when it was rewarded by universities for promotion, it discouraged academics from pursuing this. However, any future change is likely to have a significant impact, especially for those branches of knowledge less linked to the development of transfer actions, such as Arts and Humanities (Gonzalez-Sanchez, Gutierrez-Lopez, and Barrachina Palanca [2022](#page-16-15)).
#### *2. Access to the university: endogamy and power relations*
The first contact with an academic career usually began with a predoctoral or postdoctoral fellowship, which provided the opportunity to work with research teams, and even teach. Access to these scholarships was determined by the candidate's academic record, previous participation in scientific events and research papers, as well as the support of a director and a research group. However, access to a place at a university is usually achieved through two routes: as a PhD assistant after receiving accreditation from ANECA or a regional evaluation agency; or as an interim substitute, without accreditation, typically because of a department's need to cover teaching. Both are temporary contracts, but these almost guarantee the person remains in the department. In both cases, candidates are evaluated by a commission generated within the department itself, which uses official university criteria to rate the candidate's merits. Although the scales seek to be precise and well-defined, these are always open to interpretation and allow game playing in the interests of power. For example, the commission can make certain adjustments should they wish to overestimate the abilities of a candidate, thus demonstrating endogamy, inbreeding and abuse of power (Rodilla [1995)](#page-17-13). Despite the new legal frameworks, accreditation and evaluation processes, and as predicted by Sanchez-Ferrer [(1997](#page-17-3)), this space for manoeuvre has been maintained.
All participants used the term 'endogamy' to describe this phenomenon, which was seen as both a positive and negative feature of early careers. They described working in a hierarchy subject to patronage and the notion of whether 'you are in or out'. In other words, accepted and supported by those who control a majority group in a department or faculty, or conversely left out of this. Barbara spoke of: 'The feeling that you are out of the faculty and that they are not going to let you in, that even if you are the best'. Caroline noted that: 'it's not just about being good, it's about knowing which door to knock on'.
Those who had a sponsor to help them attain a position could see the positive side to this practice, while one participant was still waiting to be 'invited'. Endogamy did not mean that suitably qualified people were not placed in jobs, but the perception was still of an unfair recruitment system. In an honest reflection, Victoria noted that:
I could consider myself part of that endogamy, because I have done my thesis there and then I have continued, but I also understand in some way that they want to recruit, that is, to have
people who have worked well for them in their team and who in the work team it makes them feel more or less at ease. So, on that side, I understand that part. What I don't like is that other people from outside don't have the opportunity.
This form of endogamy is known to be widespread across higher education and includes 'academic inbreeding' where those in power hire their postgraduate student in preference to a candidate who might be better qualified (Horta [2022](#page-16-5)). The practice has advantages, including the swift integration of a new employee into the group with research-subject relevance to that group, loyalty and a measure of trust in what is essentially a low-trust environment (see Balyer and Bakay [2022](#page-16-7)). Amelia expressed a common sentiment in saying: 'I fervently believe it (…), those who run the department hire the people they want and the people they want are their doctoral students, are the ones who are their friends, their connections'. Susan spoke of knowing that:
The position is for so-and-so, it is not written down, but it is for so-and-so. So, you see yourself in a position of not asking for the position because there is going to be a battle in the department, and it brings bad vibes.
Alexander also supported 'inbreeding at times' because the candidate is already known and if that person is already seen as good, then it is human nature to value them. However, those chosen in this way, and not on merit, are aware of this, as is everyone else in the organization. Those few who have attained appointment without patronage provide a rare example for others wishing to negotiate such a pathway in their career. Interestingly, it was suggested that academics without patronage do not challenge a system in which they partially sit outside.
Patronage was also characterized by in-fighting between groups and daily battles were normal. People were observed to get upset, fight each other and hold grudges. In this battle, the rules were never clear but interpreted or modified by those in power and to their advantage. Michael pointed out that through this exercise of power, it was possible for a group to transform an entire department. These outcomes can be interpreted as an abuse of power (at least in liberal democratic Western terms) and there was a lot of investment in gaining influence to achieve a certain position. It was also suggested that a career might be doomed from the start, and conversely, Barbara pointed out that: 'The mediocre person who knows how to approach the needs of power is being rewarded'. The access door to the university is controlled by the departments and, specifically, by those groups that hold power inside them. However, access in this way is not uniform across all disciplines, and it has been seen to operate more strongly in STEM subjects (de la Torre, Perez-Esparrells, and Romero-Madrid [2021)](#page-16-16). In order for it to be truly merit-based, it was suggested that recruitment be carried out outside the departments by those with no personal interests:
Hiring should be outside. In other words, I believe that once you know who is participating, you cannot be impartial, it is impossible (…) As long as the departments continue to have the strength they have when it comes to assessing the positions, we are not going to stop being inbred. (Sophie)
However, this raises the question of who would be fit to judge the merits of a candidate outside of a subject or department context and perhaps there needs to be a more principled solution to end endogamy.

#### **Summary and conclusions**
It was clear that the professional lives of academics were overshadowed by accountability and evaluation of academic work. These were directed and shaped by different stakeholders and power groups. In an international review of university evaluation, it was argued that the growing burden of evaluation has resulted in 'a quite staggering degree of examination' (Harvey [2002,](#page-16-12) 251) and that this reflected the intrusion of the state into public life. The requirement to collect evidence in order to demonstrate competence was necessary for career access, career progression, status and remuneration, but this practice distorted academic behaviour and most found themselves acting in ways they would not otherwise have chosen. This inauthentic condition will not be unique to Spain and Harvey ([2002](#page-16-12)) argued that 'it is unlikely that there is a single country where performances are not played out' (256).
Of the two academics who seemed unaffected, one was a very successful scientist with independent income, the other was a Postdoctoral Fellow who thought that if you simply researched and taught well, you would meet what was required by the system. This proposition is based on the idea that the evaluation systems reflect good academic work, but this was not what the study showed. Evaluation measures can only address aspects of work that can easily be measured, and so compliance always distorts practice in favour of what is then rewarded. The suggestion to improve the evaluation system to better reflect desired practice did not recognize that many valued aspects of academic work are beyond easy measurement. In the pre-neoliberal era, university staff were professionals, largely trusted to get on with their jobs as experts in their subject, in teaching and research, and mainly answerable to themselves. Trust was then replaced by evidence-based compliance, and in Spain, public examination. In this context, accountability became a major additional activity to sit alongside the older teaching, research and service trinity. More importantly, when trust is replaced by accountability, which is a process closely connected to responsibility, then it makes it hard to argue against because it appears that if academics are not held to account for their actions they will behave in an 'irresponsible' manner (Biesta [2010](#page-16-3)), which, we argue, is patently absurd.
Because compliance and evaluation do not affect all staff in the same way, we suggest that an academic who has developed a research career that will allow them mobility between similar systems in different countries will be working to international standards and may then feel that local compliance is not so important, and perhaps just another bureaucratic task. Artés, Pedraja-Chaparro, and del Mar Salinas-Jiménez [(2017)](#page-16-1) showed that excellent researchers were also evaluated as the best teachers, and it is likely that highly successful researchers will be less affected by compliance, localism and endogamy. However, our study showed that most academics were not in such a position, and in addition, early career academics did not have the necessary cultural capital (Gaddis [2013)](#page-16-17) or essential systems knowledge to embark on careers that were opaque and not easily understood. This group will certainly feel more pressure to respond to evaluation as they try to meet the (often changing) criteria specified by authorities for accountability, all of which are moderated by patronage and endogamy.
The principle that academics should be accountable for their teaching and research was accepted, even though most complained about the resultant work overload and
the stress this caused to professional and personal life. However, it could be argued that acceptance normalized accountability and so changed what was initially seen as unreasonable. As such, academics appeared compliant, and none suggested the present requirements and systems be removed, despite acknowledging evaluations were constantly changing and were not good at measuring or encouraging good teaching or research. In a similar way, the embedded culture of endogamy was disliked by all, and even though it generated a culture of distrust (Melgar, Rossi, and Smith [2010)](#page-17-19), no one talked about fighting against this blatant form of corruption. We also suggest that among the academic community, there was a lack of understanding about the full impact of compliance and endogamy, especially in terms of the loss of academic freedom or the complex relationship between compliance and the broader purposes of higher education (Biesta [2010)](#page-16-3). What we might be seeing here is 'endogamous accountability', measured in terms of demonstrated loyalty to a group.
All the barriers to fairer academic career pathways illustrated an exercise of power and control, first by the government for standards in public service and second by certain power groups within universities. Before attaining tenured civil servant status, academics are more vulnerable, and the early impact on academic freedom and independence may have a lasting effect on identity as the time taken to get tenure and a permanent lectureship is long, and early habits of responding to evaluation may be hard to change. There was a genuine belief, or hope, that accountability and compliance could counter endogamy (see de la Torre, Perez-Esparrells, and Romero-Madrid [2021](#page-16-16)), but no evidence was presented to suggest this had occurred, and it is likely that truly merit-based careers were a long way off. In this sense, the Spanish system is not strictly neoliberal as the principle of competition driving performance only works if those who compete against others win through merit. In this argument, there would be no place for endogamy and any evaluation procedures would need to shift from what is easy to measure (Sutton [2017)](#page-17-0) to systems that consider a shared understanding of the broader purposes of higher education. However, merit-based systems are unlikely to combat endogamy, as criteria used in evaluation will always be open to enough interpretation to allow endogamous practices to continue. These ideas were neither directly addressed by those in the study nor in the literature, and future research may examine this relationship. With that, it has been argued that academics need to fully understand the systems they work under if they are to challenge them (see Harris [2005](#page-16-18)). In addition, we recognize that future change will require conversations between many actors, including academics, universities, professional bodies, regional agencies and national government. Only then will the academic workforce have an opportunity for unprejudiced and transparent employment conditions, with genuinely merit-based career structures and tenure status across the university sector. At the very least this would require the external audit needs of the national government to be aligned with the academics' expectations for quality work. However, the study showed the needs of academics were very different so multiple positions and identities will have to be accommodated in any change. While offering an alternative structure is well beyond the scope of this study, it was clear that the current system of accreditation and accountability imposes a bureaucratic burden on many academics without achieving its objectives around quality and fairness, which mirrors the conclusions of Sanchez-Ferrer [(1997)](#page-17-3) from 26 years earlier.
